analysis.one_liner: Extends California-style bid-based price controls to Western wholesale power markets and speeds consumer refunds.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in May 2001 and died there when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the Western electricity price crisis, this bill would have told federal regulators to apply California's plan for policing wholesale power prices to the whole Western power market, not just to hard price caps. It would have required companies selling natural gas into California to disclose how much of the price was the gas and how much was transport, barred federal orders forcing utilities to sell power into states where sellers might not get paid, let state regulators stop power exports during local shortages, and changed the law so federal rate refunds could start immediately instead of months later. It was referred to a House committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Electricity and natural gas customers in California and the broader Western power market, who during 2000-2001 were paying very high wholesale spot prices that fed into retail bills and utility bankruptcies. Faster federal refunds would have returned some of what ratepayers overpaid sooner.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Western states' electricity and gas customers

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs FERC to extend its April 2001 California market-monitoring and mitigation plan, which polices wholesale prices using competitive bids rather than inflexible caps, to all interstate wholesale electricity sales across the Western power market at all times, including resellers of wholesale power [S2][S3].

It requires companies selling bundled natural gas into California to disclose separately what they paid for the gas and what they paid for transportation, aimed at making inflated gas transportation charges visible [S2][S3].

It amends the Federal Power Act so FERC-ordered wholesale rate refunds can take effect from the date a complaint is filed rather than months later, and lets the Commission add penalties to refunds [S2][S3].
It lets state utility commissions block exports of electricity out of a utility's service area when the export would impair in-state supply during shortages [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale electricity sellers and power re-marketers, who would face bid-based price limits, faster refund liability, and possible penalties, and natural gas marketers selling into California, who would face new price disclosure rules and the end of a federal waiver on maximum transportation rates into the state.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wholesale power sellers and gas marketers

drawbacks.text: The mitigation plan would only bind utilities under FERC's jurisdiction; the bill states only that Congress intends other wholesale sellers to comply voluntarily, leaving a large loophole in a market with many out-of-jurisdiction sellers [S3].

The bill's findings declare that California should not create and run a statewide public power authority, steering the response away from a publicly owned alternative, and it gives the Secretary of Energy unilateral power to terminate the mitigation plan if supply drops [S3].

It carves out states where regulators cannot pass power costs to retail customers or where buyers may not be able to pay when due, weakening the plan's protection in exactly the distressed-market situation it was written for, and the whole mitigation section sunsets on September 30, 2002 [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a real consumer-protection bill aimed at a specific crisis: bid-based price policing, transparent gas pricing, faster refunds, and a state option to hold power home during shortages. It is not a hard price cap, and it balances its consumer provisions with seller protections like guaranteed payment. Its honest weaknesses are the voluntary-compliance loophole for out-of-jurisdiction sellers, the carve-out for states unable to pay, the Secretary's power to kill the plan, and the short sunset — all of which would have limited its bite.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on May 23, 2001, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Doug Ose of California introduced the bill on May 23, 2001, with Rep. Horn and two cosponsors total, all Republicans [S1][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which was the last action ever taken on it [S1][S5].
With no further action listed, the bill died in committee when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale electricity sellers and power re-marketers who profited from Western spot prices came out ahead: no expanded price mitigation, no mandatory fast refunds, and no penalties were ever imposed. Gas marketers selling into California likewise avoided the new disclosure rules. California's crisis was also easing by late 2001 after FERC and federal actions, which removed much of the urgency to act.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wholesale power sellers and gas marketers

for.name: Rep. Steve Horn
for.what_they_did: Joined as the named cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the May 23, 2001 referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Bush administration
against.what_they_did: Resisted broad price-control interventions in Western wholesale power markets during the 2000-2001 crisis, preferring supply-side fixes, which drained momentum for price-mitigation legislation.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes, so no party split is recorded; all three sponsors were California Republicans responding to a crisis centered on California.

industries.industry: Wholesale electricity sellers and power re-marketers
industries.note: The bill would subject their spot-market sales across the West to bid-based price mitigation, make refund liability start months earlier, and add penalties, cutting into profits earned during the 2000-2001 price spike. Those profits came directly out of what utilities and ultimately ratepayers paid.

industries.industry: Natural gas marketers selling into California
industries.note: The bill ends a federal waiver allowing bundled gas pricing into California and requires sellers to disclose the gas and transportation portions of the price, exposing inflated transportation charges that flowed into Californians' energy bills.

industries.industry: California investor-owned utilities and their ratepayers
industries.note: Faster federal refunds, Western-wide price mitigation, and a state option to block exports during shortages would have lowered costs and protected supply for utilities that were nearly insolvent and ratepayers paying the crisis prices.
